excerpt: Down at Puntan Flores, long before the war rewrote the Pacific, Japanese engineers poured concrete seaplane ramps to connect Yokohama to the south. Decades later—after the air raids, the CIA, and the jungle took over—the drains still carry the rain straight to the lagoon. A reflection on craftsmanship, memory, and what remains when empires pack up and leave.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
There is a subtle, almost forgotten art to the pouring of concrete, though few people give much thought to it nowadays. Down at Puntan Flores, on the northern hip of Saipan where the land slopes gently into the blue lagoon, the Japanese laid down seaplane ramps and drainage troughs back in the middle of the 1930s. They built them to last, mixing stone and sand with a deliberate, painstaking care that seems almost gentle when set against what came later. If you walk through Lower Base today—past the hum of the power plant and the tangle of tropical scrub—you can still find those drains. They are clear, level, and after ninety years of salt air and torrential rain, they still carry water away precisely as they were drawn to do.

A few years back, at a history conference in the Marianas, archaeologist David G. DeFant showed some slides of the site. He spoke of the surviving work and called it "remarkable." The concrete poured in 1934 had none of the frantic, slapdash quality of the bunkers thrown up a decade later when the American fleet was already on the horizon. Those early structures belonged to a different mind, and a different, slower tempo of living.

History in this corner of the Pacific is usually told in sudden, violent bursts, but the story of Puntan Flores began in simple prose. Under the League of Nations mandate, the port was already humming with commerce. Sugar brought people—tens of thousands of Okinawan families moving south to work the fields, until the foreign population swelled from a couple hundred under the Germans to nearly sixty thousand.

When the seaplane base was laid out in 1934, it was fundamentally a civilian affair—a maritime outpost connecting Yokohama to Saipan, Palau, Chuuk, and Jaluit. Flying boats operated by Dai Nippon Koku drifted down into the calm waters of the bay, bringing mail, cargo, and passengers on a schedule that felt reassuringly permanent. There were subtle arguments in Geneva and Washington about whether Japan was surreptitiously militarizing the islands, prompting Tokyo to walk out of the League. Yet on the ground at Puntan Flores, the work remained thorough, orderly, and largely unhurried.

Then, as it always seems to do when nations prepare for war, the rhythm shifted. Around 1939, the military took over. What had been a single concrete ramp grew into a sprawling warren of sixty-five buildings—steel hangars, underground magazines, fuel bunkers, and air-raid shelters. You could read the coming urgency in the masonry itself. The later additions lacked the finesse of the early work; fine edges disappeared, replaced by rough aggregate and hurried forms.

When the invasion came in June of 1944, the island changed hands, but the geography remained stubbornly useful. The Americans took Puntan Flores, widened the aprons to hold their heavier aircraft, and converted a fuel bunker into a radio tower. Decades later, when the CIA set up a clandestine facility on the heights of Capitol Hill, the ridge became known as "Upper Base," and the old seaplane ramp below inherited the plain, utilitarian name it carries today: Lower Base.

DeFant noted, with a scholar’s soft regret, that almost everything we know about Puntan Flores comes from wartime intelligence dossiers—documents that tend to reduce complex human landscapes to targets, fuel capacities, and troop strength. They leave out the Japanese engineers who calculated the pitch of those drains, and the local hands who hauled the aggregate under a hot sun.

It is easy to look at an overgrown strip of concrete and see only a ruin. But if you stand by the water's edge at Puntan Flores long enough, past the industrial clutter, you realize you are looking at a quiet ledger of human ambition. The wars came and went, the empires dissolved, and the CIA packed up its filing cabinets and departed. What remains, half-buried under the vines, is the smooth, solid curve of an old drainage ditch—still straight, still square, and still doing its modest job, waiting for the rain.
title: The Seaplanes of Puntan Flores
